how: Calls recruited members to start a flag, defend existing work, and join a replacement attempt.
Members distinguished nominal subscribers from active users and described limited attention during the offseason.
A member answered ongoing building with a bare commitment to join.
A bare commitment appears among the answers to the build, supporting one acceptance form without establishing unwritten placing.
Willing acceptance need not be bare or ask nothing back when a volunteer requires someone to supply a starting place.
A conditional volunteer required a starting place before contributing, so an invitation alone did not supply an actionable target.
Participants clarified whether Place meant the canvas or a local bar before an invitation could be understood consistently.
Members proposed the flag and later recruited helpers around a little twelve without evidence of formal appointment.
A replacement starter recruited helpers into a specific new thread and then coordinated their border work.
Participants proposed alternative sizes and colors, disputed plans, and sequenced common work before settling the remaining color choice.
Members reported converting an existing numeral and preparing a new field while its border progressed.
Recruitment and later building reports establish sequence, but the preserved passages do not identify which call caused members to place.
Builders requested a copyable end product and received an updated design, then sought one version in the opening post.
A posted template settles design only with continued acceptance, because competing plans, recoloring, and a challenge to finality reopened alignment.
Builders could prioritize the shared outline and numeral while deferring a disputed color to majority preference.
Members used spare accounts to add placing effort, without establishing scripts or bots.
A single case cannot test the population claim, and organizer credit plus proposed majority preference does not determine formal appointment or completed voting.
Members protected an existing twelve through calls for helpers, repeated placing, and overnight defense.
A builder explicitly treated getting a twelve onto the canvas as the reason to switch to protecting it.
Spare accounts accompanied defense, but their users did not state that attack pressure caused adoption beyond single-account capacity.
Participants traced alleged attackers, corrected one opponent's identity, and disputed blame by distinguishing random users from a whole fan group.
Explanations of destruction remained competing attributions rather than an agreed cause.
A mutual-defense proposal was challenged, narrowed to non-interference, and accepted with a one-pixel warning.
A proposed partnership became acceptable only when reframed as not interfering with each other's work.
Participants agreed to spare another builder and repaired neighboring pixels while asking their own fans to behave.
A member replied to the truce warning with reported repairs and a promise to restrain fellow fans, without proving collective compliance.
A proposed move during a constant battle elicited advice to ask a neighboring group for permission and integrate its color.
Members repaired neighboring colors and promised further restoration, establishing help without requiring a completed reciprocal bargain.
Strain prompted proposed outside alliances, but incoming assistance cannot be inferred from an unanswered proposal.
Repair followed negotiation, but reciprocal exchange remains unresolved because only one side's repair and promises are evidenced.
Alliance proposals and an accepted non-interference limit do not establish an adopted coalition or sustained joint defense.
Defense pressure can produce alliance proposals that stop at non-interference, so coalition formation requires evidence of accepted joint defense.
An organizer reported diplomacy, answered a neighbor, repaired damage, and tried to restrain fellow fans.
Participants disputed approval and claimed prior allocation, instantiating the candidate's contested permission component.
Contested allocation claims establish neither accepted host authority nor confirmed residence on a host's mark.
Rejecting ownership of canvas space does not establish a dispute over who may commit members to an agreement.
Negotiation and approval disputes leave the proposed transition to challenging a representative's binding authority unobserved.
Reported destruction prompted offers to rebuild elsewhere and another attempt at a smaller mark.
An organizer explicitly tied inability to face three neighboring groups to the instruction to move right.
An organizer requested withdrawal of repair so decay would persuade defenders that moving was best.
A shortage judgment could require changing defenders' attachment to the current mark before they stopped maintaining it and accepted relocation.
Relocation overlapped continued blue filling and preparation of a new field, making rebuilding part of the move rather than a wholly separate restart.
A sports community proposed its familiar twelve and invoked regional pride as the basis for a shared canvas mark.
Prior sports rivalry entered coexistence talk through the wish for a regional area and a joke about divisional rivals.
Hostile fan rhetoric in the moderator joke and separate canvas restraint do not establish a turn using prior rivalry to call for an attack.
The host staged an everyone-is-moderator takeover and explained confused reactions as April Fools.
Members performed granted powers through imagined bans, stickies, absurd rules, and complaints that the powers were unreal.
Seeing the host's joke depended on interface access when a confused mobile user was directed to a desktop browser.
The performance continued through mutiny and allegiance after an announcement that the temporary moderator experiment had ended.

statement: Resuming personal conversation from a temporary-role exchange
how: A temporary-role status check shifted into an ordinary personal catch-up without an evidenced effect on canvas organizing.
Moderation gathered recurring canvas posts into one organizing thread.
The consolidating post explicitly explained its action as a response to repeated new threads.
Members thanked the organizer, described fun helping, and celebrated the flag's endurance.
Members marked closure and recorded divergent accounts of survival, appearance, effort, and disappointment.
Celebration and credit need not rest on an agreed finished object when members evaluate the same result as both terrible and strong.
Closure and survival reports preceded later gratitude, so recording cannot be presumed to originate in a prior shared completion ritual.
An organizer valued the contested location itself as interesting, preserving an evaluation of the experience beyond the mark's final appearance.
Contrasting evaluations do not establish a dispute over cleanup, an authoritative preserved version, or public correction of the event's history.
A member redirected potential builders toward a successor canvas.
An individual's successor-canvas redirect does not establish collective adoption or successful continuation.
Recording preceded the redirect, but no preserved passage attributes continuation to keeping a record of the original work.
Members reported converting existing marks, while the target's ownership and any coordinated rival-directed attack remained unresolved.
Participants carried the contest in talk through overlap accusations, accounts of tit-for-tat changes, and conflicting descriptions of attack and recovery.
Recruitment and reported interference do not establish that a call turned contributors toward attacking a rival.
Repair and cost-based restraint answer reported damage, but an antecedent attack-call-to-refusal pair is not preserved.
Neighbor negotiation is visible without evidence that an attack call prompted it.
Accusations and contest talk do not identify an attack call that generated them.
